utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. We will move into private session for two reasons. First, we have a procedural matter to deal with, and after that we'll continue to hear the evidence of the witness who is at present giving testimony, and that testimony, at least this part, which will take quite a while, will be heard in private session. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Sacic, the questions I'll put to you are dealing with the special police involved in combat operations, and I'll focus on Operation Storm. First of all, could you describe the uniforms that were worn by the special police when they took part in combat operations in Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had green uniforms, the active-duty police had green uniforms. But sometimes a reservist might have a camouflage uniform, but that was very, very infrequent. As a rule, they had solid green uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did they have any insignia which would identify them as belonging to special police units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In combat, yes. To ensure that they would not be victims of friendly fire, they had some kind of ribbons tied on their shoulder patch. They could be green or blue or yellow, so something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did they have any other patches or whatever that could identify them as such?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had a patch on their sleeve. There would be a sword and lightning on the left sleeve, whereas on the right sleeve they would have a round patch which would say "Special Police of the Republic of Croatia MUP." And on their breast, there would be the words "Special Police."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to show you some pictures. Could we have P324 on our screens, the second page. Could you look at the picture, and could you tell us whether this was someone wearing a uniform as used by the special police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am certain, 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we move to the first page. The person who is carrying something and who's standing closest to the blue truck, is that the uniform of the special police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I cannot really see the patch on the right sleeve or shoulder. There should be something there. But it is a green uniform, and the shoes are standard-issue special police, and I can even see that there's a sort of yellow ribbon on his shoulder, so I could assume that perhaps this was that uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I take you to Exhibit P325. Could that be brought on the screen, second. Do you recognise those uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. These are special police uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we move to the third page of this document. Same question for the person who is standing --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that you're referring to the person who can be seen as the third to the left of the person with the white clothing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They're all special police members.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say "they're all," may I take it that you do not include the person in the white clothing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You do include the four persons standing left to him, of which one has a kind of a red band around his head?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Lucko unit, were they wearing similar uniforms or the same uniforms as we have seen on these pictures?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Only if somebody had another uniform in case he was caught in the rain, so the rain overcoat could be camouflaged. So, theoretically, there may have been some pieces with a camouflage pattern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you told us that sometimes people who didn't have the plain green uniform, that they might have been dressed, although being a member of the special police, in camouflage uniforms, and that the same could happen under rainy circumstances, where a kind of an overcoat was used or at least coverage against the rain, a cover against the rain. Now, the Chamber has heard evidence that for some combat operations, the special police was attached to the Croatian Army forces, the HV forces. Would they still wear the same uniforms, or would they then wear different uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The rule was to wear green uniforms always. Exceptionally, individuals could wear a different uniform, such as -- in that case, where they would change into a reserve uniform, but the rule was a green uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, taking you back to the early stages of Operation Storm, could you tell us, where were you between the 5th and the 9th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 5th of August, at 1600 hours, I was in Gracac, until the following morning, the 6th, probably until 7.00 or 8.00. And then on the 6th, I suppose I set out for Bruvno.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us where you were before 4.00 p.m. on that 5th of August?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the early-morning hours, that is, all day from the 4th, until 12.00 on the 5th of August, I was at the top of the Velebit, on my forward command post which was on Mali Golic. That's a mountain. Around 11.00 or 11.05, I received information that the units of the special police had put under their control the road to Gracac. I immediately issued instructions to my staff that they should start packing everything up, all communications devices and other equipment, and that we would go to Gracac, which we did. The trip lasted from about 1300 until 1600 hours, when we arrived in Gracac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you said you received information that the units of the special police had put under their control the road to Gracac. Is that the Gospic-Gracac road, or is it another road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that's another road, the road through the Velebit area, from Bukva to Mali Alan, Kraljicina Vrata, that's a pass, and an old, unpaved road descends to Gracac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you tell us which units had taken control of that road, which special police units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About two and a half thousand special police troops must have moved along that road or must have taken that road, carrying out their tasks, so the road remained in the rear, and the road descended to Sveti Rok, where there was a junction with the tarmac road from Sveti Rok to Gracac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I ask you about various units, could you tell us whether they were involved in this operation? The Bjelovar-Bilogora [phoen] unit, could you tell us --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, they carried out their task honourably, courageously and honourably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did they take the town of Loncari? Did they take control of that town, as far as you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Loncari? I don't know that place, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does the name "Lovinac" ring a bell with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it does. I know Lovinac. It's a village not far from Sveti Rok.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know which unit took control of that village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There must have been more than one unit. I would have to guess, but there was a unit made up of people who hailed from Lovinac. And that unit was one of ours, and they may have been the ones. I cannot be specific at the moment. But if you could show me a document, I believe that would remind me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, instead of showing you all kind of documents: Lika Sen's unit, were they among those?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean a unit by the name of Lika Senj? No. Tigar-Gospic, yes; but Lika Senj, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether the Lucko unit was in any way involved or was ever located in Lovinac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to plan, Lucko should have been along one of the directions. They descended from the top of Velebit down to Sveti Rok, but whether they, indeed, entered Lovinac, I couldn't tell, Your Honour. Because I did prepare for this testimony, but there is such a huge amount of information, thousands of pages, so I cannot be that specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm asking you what you can tell us from your memory. Of course, we have seen quite a lot of documents. The Rijeka unit, could you tell us where they were on that morning of the 5th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that. They were also on that axis. I think it was the fourth auxiliary axis. They also came down from Velebit, and they went to the Sveti Rok-Medak road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Same question for the Zagreb unit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Special Police Unit Alpha from Zagreb, yes. Their commander, Zoran Cvrk, commanded one of the axes of advance. And on that axis, there was the ATJ Lucko unit, I remember. It was one of the units on that axis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Same questions for the Zabok unit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember them too. They were also on that axis of advance. I believe it may have been the third auxiliary axis or the fourth. The others who were involved were the Special Police Unit Tigar, Tiger, from Gospic, and part of the Vukovar-Srijem unit, Vinkovci, to be more specific. Then part of the Sisak Moslavina unit, but I'm not sure whether they were from Moslavina or Sisak proper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Dubrava Neretva unit, could you tell us whether they were among the units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dubrava Neretva, no. Maybe Grof from Dubrovnik. There weren't many of them, 25 only. They may have been involved as intervention unit, but most certainly not under the name of Dubrava Neretva. They could have been the special police unit of the Dubrovnik-Neretva Police Administration, and their logo was -- or, rather, their name -- the name by which they were known was "Grof," which means "Count."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'd say they were a unit from the Dubrava Neretva Police Administration, but they were not called by that name, but they had their own name, "Grof," as you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. No, no. Their name was the Special Police Unit of the Dubrovnik-Neretva Police Administration. "Grof" was an additional name. They were also known as "Grof," such as with other units that were known as "Tiger" or something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They were nicknames for the unit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's what they liked. Everybody had their own nickname, if we can call it that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, when did these units, if they did, take control over Gracac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not all these units. As far as I remember and as far as I know, the center of Gracac was put under the control of the special police of the Vukovar-Srijem Police Administration, more specifically the Delta unit from Zupanja. And the road, access road from Ricica to Gracac was under the control partly of the Bijelovarska-Bilogorska unit, and the surrounding hills were under the control of the Bak unit of the Istria Police Administration. They entered the area with the first echelon around 1100 or 1105 on the 5th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're talking about the first echelon. The second echelon arrived at what time in Gracac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The task at the time was to have as few forces in Gracac as possible. The second echelon went to the areas outside of Gracac, the area to the south of Gracac, at the foot of Mount Velebit. And to the north of Gracac, there were also some forces from the second echelon. Some forces were at the crossroads from Gracac to Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You told us that you went in the -- first of all, when you arrived in Gracac, what did you do? What was your task at that moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Find a place for our headquarters and link up with the operation commander, General Markac, and assigned for my forward command post. I didn't take much time. As soon as he got to Gracac, I'm positive that we went to the courthouse. It's not really at the very center of Gracac, but it's easily accessible on a street.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is that where you established your headquarters for the time being or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Our communications people started working immediately. They placed their emitters and receivers. The logistics people also did their part of the work. There was some furniture there, and everything was ready to use soon. As soon as 1800 hours, I think we were visited by the minister of the interior, Mr. Ivan Jarnjak, and I reported to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you told us that -- you said the next day you went to -- you proceeded in the direction of Bruvno. This Chamber received evidence that some of the troops that -- some of the units that moved on to Bruvno, that they stayed at Stikada for approximately one day. Is that something you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is Stikada just west of Gracac; is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were there any special police units that moved in the direction of Gospic, leaving Gracac on that same 5th of August?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, there were such units, and they mostly moved along the main road, that is, west of Gracac, from the Sveti Rok-Medak access, and further on to Licki Ribnik, where they joined up with HV forces around 2200 hours which were advancing from the direction of Gospic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, do you know what HV forces or what HV units it were where they joined up with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I suppose they were local units from Gospic, possibly a home guards regiment, but this -- I cannot really say which forces. That would be guess-work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you were operating under the command of what military district, if you were under the command of any military district, for this combat operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To me, as Chief of Staff, that was irrelevant. I was under the command of the operation commander, Mladen Markac, all the time. And as Chief of Staff, there was no need for me to communicate directly with any military district. My commander did that at a higher level. He would know the details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you not know under whose operational command General Markac was at the time, which -- even if you did not have to communicate directly with any military district, do you know -- Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, just by way of clarification, I think -- I don't know if you want to put this objection in front of the witness. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know what the objection is. Therefore, I don't know --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, I think it's an undisputed fact that the special police was not under any military district.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Undisputed?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: We don't dispute it, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't dispute it. Then we don't have to go into that area. I leave the question as it is and move on, move on to that next day. It seems that your recollection is now that you didn't move the next day in the direction of Bruvno, but the day after that. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it seems that I was in Gracac on the 6th. In the late-evening hours of the 5th, some units, as instructed by the chief of General Staff of the HV, Mr. Zvonimir Cervenko -- General Cervenko, which instructions were passed on to me by my commander, General Mladen Markac, these units were supposed to be sent to Bruvno at night, and that's what happened, because we received information that there was a tank platoon -- an enemy tank platoon there and that they were planning on carrying out a counter-attack. So we were worried about that, and our units arrived in Bruvno around 2300 hours. And as far as I remember, they -- there was no confrontation on the way there. Since special police units on the 5th had carried out more tasks than had been expected of them, we were in a sweep, to put it that way, and that's why our commander assigned us new tasks. And I was seeing to it that the prerequisites for the carrying out of those tasks be in place with my collaborators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What did the -- you said some units were sent to Bruvno at night. First question: After they had arrived in Bruvno, where did they go after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they just deployed in a circular defence position in order to spend the night there and in order to actually prepare everything to set up a repeater there, and they were also instructed that they can go on leave, of course, with all the provisions for security that are normal under such wartime conditions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And after they had done all that, could you tell us, from Bruvno -- you said you moved to Bruvno on the, well, 6th or the 7th. Now, how did the units move on from Bruvno on that day, which whether you call it axis or whatever you call it, how did they move? Perhaps I'll first ask you, how did they end up at the end of that day, the 7th of August? Where did they -- what places did they finally reach?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, for my own coherence, I would appreciate it if you allow me to start from the very beginning, if that's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So on the 6th, we prepare the documents, and we showed it to the commander, to our esteemed general. And then we were to further develop the -- within -- according to the orders by General Cervenko, our units, our police units, were supposed to reach the border with Bosnia and Herzegovina, the state borders, as soon as possible. The shortest route in order to carry that out, pursuant to the proposal put forth by our headquarters, our staff and our general, would be the Bruvno, Mazin, Gornji and Donji Lapac, and Boricevac axis; in other words, in the direction of the Una River. For that, it was necessary to employ a significant number of troops, I think even five or six battalions of the special police, but we also had two auxiliary axis. General Markac felt that we were supposed to make sure to provide for our flanks, and he ordered that one battalion of the forces should head in the direction of Udbine; whereas another battalion of the special police would set out from Gracac, but this was already on the 6th - I am quite sure of that - towards Otric in order to join up the Croatian Army forces. And there was another place where they were supposed to join up the Croatian Army forces. That was in Udbine. And since all these plans had been drawn up, on the 7th we set out very early in the morning, perhaps already at 6.00, as I already described earlier. And within the usual -- the normal chain of command, with clear chains of commands, the commanders along these axis were subordinated directly to me and in direct contact with me. I had my own mobile staff in a command vehicle, and I was periodically -- or, rather, I periodically informed, about all the key elements and key issues, General Markac, but he also had his own communications system and he could monitor or follow everything that was going on, and he could also get in touch with me whenever he needed to. But as for the ongoing issues that I felt should be resolved between me and the commanders, I would proceed to do that on my own, and then perhaps after a while, maybe even an hour later, I would inform him of that. But sometimes, if I did not consider it of sufficient significance, I would not even mention the actions that were taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, the shortest route to Donji Lapac by Bruvno, Mazin, Gornji Lapac, and then Donji Lapac is clear to me. Now, you said some of the units would take a different direction. You mentioned Udbina, and then from Udbina in the direction of Donji Lapac, after having joined with the HV units. Now, would they go to -- please correct me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. When these forces reached Udbina, and this was the special police unit from Karlovac, I believe, and maybe part of Sisak units, their destination was Udbina alone and the deployment in circular defence position on the foot -- in the hills. Their task was not to go to Gornji or Donji Lapac, because that would have been too difficult for them. The terrain was mountainous, and it would be about 30 kilometres or so, so they just deployed there. So, so much about them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And going in the direction of Udbina, would they first go to Bruvno and then, if you say so, to -- then further move in a northwesterly direction; is that how they went there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they advanced from Bruvno towards Udbina. That was the most logical route. And our concentrated forces advanced from Bruvno towards Mazin and upward to Gornji Lapac, as I've already mentioned, where one part of the troops actually split and headed towards the northerly forest or wooded areas, and they were supposed to cover that in an infantry advance. There was some 300, I believe, troops, infantry troops. So they were then supposed, in a forced march, to reach Donji Lapac or, rather, to reach the outskirts of Donji Lapac, the approaches of Donji Lapac; whereas the main forces were advancing along an asphalt road towards Gornji Lapac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take you to a map of that area to especially understand the last part of your answer. Could I have P190 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would truly appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I will give some further instructions as where to zoom in. Maps take a while, Mr. Sacic. Could we zoom in and focus on the right top corner, to start with. That's the left top corner, from what I am -- yes, we see. Could you move a little bit further. Yes. Could we further zoom in on that area step by step, please. Yes, if we could zoom in. A little bit more to the north, further up. That seems not to be -- could we move the -- yes, Madam Registrar. Yes. Could we now move the whole of the picture a little bit to the left, and let's stop there. Can you see it on the your screen, Mr. Sacic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you see Donji Lapac, which is approximately at the middle of the map on the top?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you see Gornji Lapac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, could you by -- tell us how the -- in view of your last answer, and perhaps give us the names you can see on the map, how the units moved from Gornji Lapac to Donji Lapac and what route they took? If not all the same route, as I understood from your answer, tell us how some of them moved and how others moved.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I can say with certainty that we set off from Mazin --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to have the map again on the screen, and we start the exercise again. Could we move -- yes. Zoom in further. Yes, I think we are back again. Let's look --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we are. Well, I understood your question. So the main forces --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. You started in Mazin. I see Mazin now as a --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- relatively small village which is located just a bit south-west of the center of the map we have before us. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So we set out from Mazin towards Potselo, as I can see up there, and then we followed the road. It says "Zuldovaca." It's some kind of mountain pass there. And then you can see there are these hairpin bends in the road towards Gornji Lapac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then our forces proceeded up the main road towards Donji Lapac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To be clear, that's the road which goes from Gornji Lapac in a northwesterly direction up to the point where it reads "Donji Lapac," "D. Lapac." Did all the troops go on that main road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct -- no, not all troops. As I already said, some of the troops went through the wooded area. It was a very difficult terrain with no roads, and I think they forked away very soon, perhaps from Mazin Polje, to the left towards this hill, Javornik, where you can see the wood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have not found that word yet. Mr. Usher, could you please provide the witness with the plan so that he can --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So to the north, Javornik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see -- is that close to a village which is called "Orahovac"? Is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I shouldn't really speak off the top of my head. Perhaps the best thing would be if I could have that order or the report, I could tell you exactly, because that would specify exactly the axis and every village and road, because I can't really remember all those details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will try to find that order, but we'll first have a break. And did you mention Ajdukovic before, or is that what you referred to? Could you already -- you mentioned a certain name. Could we ask already --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The outskirts, the approaches to Donji Lapac, that's what I mentioned. But that's easily checked in -- you can see it in the report following Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll continue with that after the break. But you just mentioned a name, and could I invite Mr. Usher already to give you the pen to -- apparently, there was a -- could you please circle the place you just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, here [marks], I mentioned Javornik. Now I understood what you meant. So this is that part that I circled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll continue after the break. We'll have a break, and we'll resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Sacic, I'm struggling with my screen. Could one of the technicians assist me. Mr. Mikulicic, if you could assist the Chamber, that would be appreciated. What I found at this moment, Mr. Sacic, is an order dated the 6th of August, which says -- which is under the heading "Order to continue combat operations in D plus 2," and I read in paragraph 3 the following: "Special units of the MUP, upon capturing the Bruvno and Malovan saddles, continue the attack towards Donji Lapac and capture this area in co-ordination with the forces of the Gospic Military District on the left flank and the forces of the Split Military District on the right flank." Mr. Mikulicic, my problem is that during breaks, I'm locked in here, so I can't at that moment consult my e-court in my office anymore. My apologies, Mr. Sacic, but my computer was not very -- any further detailed orders, Mr. Mikulicic? Do you have them or --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, there was an order titled "D plus 1, D plus 2," and the following orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But isn't that D plus 1 for the first day and --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No, D plus 1 is not for the first day. In fact, D plus 1 is after the Gracac, so it will be the third day, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I mean D plus 2, which orders --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: D plus 2 is Order D552.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I have just read from that one. Is there a later or more detailed order?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes. On that topic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On that topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No, no. The following order is D plus 3, but it refers to some other territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Sacic, I'll take you back to the map. I just read to you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "Upon capturing the Bruvno and Malovan saddles." Now, where Bruvno is, is relatively clear to us. Now, could you tell us where the Malovan saddles are?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a -- we cannot see it here. It's to the right, in the lower right, toward Otric probably. Can we raise the map a little? In this part, it should be around here [indicates].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we now zoom out again, but not as much as we --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can anybody help me? Otric --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you tell us to go more south or -- what we have at this moment is we see is "Udbina" --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right. It should be Malovan. It's up here in this part from Gracac to Otric, but I ask for assistance. There are people who know this better. The general is laughing, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Tell us whether we have to go more south or east or west or north in order to find it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, let's go to the Gracac-Otric road, and we'll find it. It should be there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Tell us to go down, left, right, or up, and then we'll try to get you there, if you tell us. And then we'll ask the assistance of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand. Raise it a bit, please. Good. We found Gracac. Here it is. Raise it some more. I would fail a geography exam. I apologise. Malovan should be hereabouts [indicates], but the story about Malovan doesn't matter to me at all. Of course, I know of that hill or mountain. Could somebody help me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If I may assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because I'm a bit confused about going from --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Well, if you go -- if you go east of Gracac and a little bit south, you will see, almost in the middle of the screen, red-coloured letters "WK." Just above that capital letters, you will see Malovan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just a second. Gracac, and then you said further ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If you go from Gracac to the right side, that means to the east, and a little bit -- yes, now we'll see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "WK," is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, "WK" on the left side of the screen, and above these letters is "Malovan."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yeah, that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm still a bit surprised.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thanks a lot. Thanks a lot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's not very much in the direction of Donji Lapac, is it? I try to understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's in the direction of Otric, as I said initially, and I'm proud of myself now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's always good. At the end of the day, it's always good --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And the general can be proud of me for not making a mistake here, but I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, apparently that's not in the direction of Donji Lapac, and I would like to focus on before the break. And can we move a little bit further up on the map. Further, further, further, further. Yes, further up, and now a little bit further to -- a little bit further up and a little bit further to the left. A little bit more, yes. Now further up; not too much, not too much. Yes, there we are. The Bruvno saddles, do you know where that is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course. It can be seen. It's on the left, in this corner [indicates]. If we position it in relation to Mazinsko Polje, it's north-west of that, a field. There is "Bruvanski" and, and then below that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see "Mazinsko Polje," and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. And then go back to the left and down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To the left and down, that is where I read "Cerovac Bruvanski." Is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, correct. And a bit further left and down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and then we get to Bruvno, isn't it? That's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, how do I have to understand this? Where you told us that part of the units would go Bruvno-Mazin-Dobroselo-Gorji Lapac-Donji Lapac. Now you said another -- some other units would go in a different way. Is there any way you could indicate on this map, if only by what area, approximately, they went through when going in the direction, as I understood you well, of Donji Lapac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that would be, as I mentioned, Javornik, which I circled --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That has not been saved. Could we try to do that again. Mr. Usher, could you assist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I touch the screen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll get a pen, and you'll be invited. But given you said -- what name did you just mention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Javornik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please circle "Javornik"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]. That's this wider area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. Now, how would these units get from Javornik approximately to Donji Lapac? Could you give us an indication, if you know? It seems a rather mountainous area there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that's exactly the problem. It would seem that they -- [marks]. This is the route they took, this should be it through the forested area, but don't take my word for it. I think this must have been the axis. Of course, the units had to consider the terrain, so they may have strayed a bit from this line. But this is the rough axis. The detailed plan of movement should be -- it should be possible to find it on our maps. I don't have every detail in my memory, but it should be as indicated. I apologise if I made a mistake, but the majority of forces took this route [marks]. Then we had protection on our left flank. And then some forces went to Udbina. Possibly, there was an auxiliary axis that went like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, what I do understand, that is the majority of the troops took the main road, which is the blue line you've drawn at the right-hand side; whereas a smaller number of units --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They took the more difficult route, and my deputy, Zdravko Janjic was the leader of those forces. That was very difficult, forbidding terrain. Some 400 special police members moved along that axis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand that they managed finally to get through the difficult terrain and then approximately, as you indicated by this blue line, without perhaps great precision -- what could be the margin left and right of the left line? Would it have been one kilometre, two kilometres, that you may have been mistaken? Or is this approximately what you would consider to be the route they would have taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember that as Chief of Staff, I drew that direction personally on the 6th, and I'm certain that I took part in defining that axis. So now I'll be ashamed if I made a mistake, but I remember Javornik and the Javornik woods. I'm not sure whether Ajdukovic Brdo was also on that axis, but I believe that this should be it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, were there any other forces, whether special police forces or HV forces, or whatever forces you would have co-ordinated with in this area? That means the Javornik and then up to the north to Donji Lapac area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm 100 per cent sure that there were no other forces at the time, because we were the first Croatian forces to advance here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So there were no HV troops going in that -- through that same area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not -- not as far as I remember, no, certainly not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May this marked map be saved and assigned a number. If there are any problems, Madam Registrar, then we will assign that number at a later stage, as long as it is saved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Saving causes some problem. We should not touch the screen any more from now on until the moment that the map has been saved. Mr. Sacic, did you go with the units in the direction of Donji Lapac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. I took the main road, Mazin-Mazinsko Polje-Zubovaca, up to those hip and bends towards Gornji Lapac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, earlier we have received evidence that units would go through Dobroselo as well. Now, the main road with the hairpins goes directly to Gornji Lapac. Was there any unit that went through Dobroselo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was their objective to reach Dobroselo. That may have been a battalion of 300 men, and they, indeed, reached the place. Now, I'm not sure whether they took the main road to Gornji Lapac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was a bit worried about your markings perhaps being lost, Mr. Sacic, but apparently they're not lost. Madam Registrar, the number assigned to the marked map would be --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit C4, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: C4 is admitted into evidence. Yes, they would reach Dobroselo from Gornji Lapac, or would they go through Dobroselo and then to Gornji Lapac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, no. The main forces went to Gornji Lapac. I'm sure of that, because I was there myself. The only issue now is whether one group -- or, in fact, it's certain that one group moved from Gornji Lapac to the south, to Dobroselo, along the main road, and I assume that for security reasons a group followed the edges of the foothills here. We see the place called Divoselo. But at any case, they were going along the road because the road was frequently under attack, exposed to artillery attacks, so we all avoided it as much as we could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, talking about artillery attacks, did you receive, well, let's say, on -- from the beginning, before you entered Gracac, did you receive artillery support when moving to Gracac, and later from Gracac, Bruvno, Donji Lapac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we had sustained support. We had a very developed system. It was very efficient, and the commander was extremely -- the chief of artillery was extremely competent and capable, Commander Josip Turkalj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So this was artillery provided by the special police. It was not any outside artillery unit, but it was the artillery unit -- where were they located during these days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they had many difficulties in those days, because we advanced very fast, and they had difficulty with that. And frequently they were too far forward, exposed, so that I can't tell you where exactly they were. But Mr. Turkalj did a brilliant job, and I know that he used to complain to me. He criticised me, saying that he should have been advised at least a few hours earlier of what was expected of him and where, but I just couldn't do it because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us further details about where the artillery batteries moved, where they were located, if you remember.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they had their own independent logistics, so they had transport trucks, and there was a special unit that was escorting them, a reserve unit, who were just in charge of that, and they were highly qualified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Sacic, would you please focus your answer on my question. I asked you whether you knew where the locations of the batteries were. Were they -- did they stay behind? Where -- let's say at the beginning of the operation, where was the -- how many artillery batteries did you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we had six 128-millimetre mortar batteries, we had multiple rocket-launchers, 75-millimetre mortars, and we had a lot of fire-power that was necessary in order to soften the forward line -- the enemy's forward line, and they were deployed at the appropriate distance from the line of contact. They operated on call either from the axis commander, or the axis commander would then request that I help by conveying this request for artillery support. So that's how it worked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you're talking about the axis commander, that would be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, those were commanders, in any case, of special police units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you say the commander of the specific unit, and we mentioned quite a number of those units before, that they would call for the artillery support?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, sometimes even subordinate officers, perhaps his -- the commander's deputy, who at a given time found himself in tight spot, militarily speaking; they ran, for instance, into a bunker or into a stronghold, enemy stronghold, or perhaps they observed a rocket unit -- enemy rocket unit, where they needed support. So these were the situations that we usually ran into, and this type of communication was what we usually had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, how were the targets described, or were there any lists, or was it just on the basis of the observation of the unit commander, or how did this work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As the special police force, we were a unit that was offensive, and we could advance very fast, and it was necessary for our observers to see where it was, where there was a stronghold, and then we would send, by coded messages, information, and with specific information as to where exactly they needed to open fire. So this was the objective. We didn't have any strategic shellings or actions. We only used them to clear the passage. So if there was an obstacle on our way, then they would assist in facilitating our movement forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did any pre-defined target lists exist which were used when calling for artillery support?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We -- it is quite certain that Mr. Turkalj could tell you more about the pre-defined targets. I really could not name them at this point, nor would I want to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to name them. My question was: Were there any such pre-defined target lists that did exist and were used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I assume so. I assume, in fact, that we had -- for instance, there was a railway line, Gracac-Medak, where there was an occasion train that would move along that railway with enemy artillery, and of course at some point I'm sure that that railway line would have been a target of our artillery. I'm just giving this by way of example. Perhaps there would be a military staff or headquarters somewhere that would be a target, but these are concrete targets that you can probably find exact information, specific information about from people who are more competent than I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, I'm not primarily asking about whether such targets existed and where they were, but I'm asking whether any pre-defined targets, such as the one you mentioned, were available, or lists -- or lists saying, "Railway," or "Crossroads." Did such lists, with the coordinates --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand. The first -- the front-line, the enemy line, was certainly the target of our artillery. I can remember that. I'm quite certain of that. As for anything else that I could say now, it would just be guess-work, and I really wouldn't want to engage in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, my question is not what the targets were, and I'm not inviting you to guess, but whether there were any lists, short or long, saying "Railway X, Y, Z," or "Headquarters of Counter-Intelligence, X, Y, Z." Did such lists with the co-ordinates, did they exist and were they used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only on the first day. Only on the first day, when we had to break through the first line, there must have been such lists of strongholds, enemy strongholds, such as the places where we thought that there was a concentration of enemy forces. But as for others, I think there were no such lists, that they were selected ad hoc when our units ran into some kind of obstacle, then they would call for artillery support.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say the first day, looking at the progress that was made. Would that go up to Gracac, for example? I mean, for example, "Crossroads in Gracac, X, Y, Z, or "Police station in Gracac," or whatever target there would have been, would --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, on Velebit -- on the Velebit front-line, it is certain that they existed, because we had strong enemy forces there that offered firm resistance. But on the communication lines and on the foot of the mountain, it was very difficult -- it was very important to define exactly the target and then request -- for instance, if a request was sent to me, then my subordinates would have to describe exactly what was going on there, whether this was a strong point of resistance, whether there were fortifications there, or things to that effect. So it wasn't given -- it wasn't -- such support was not provided without a specific reason provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That still does not answer my question. You said there must have been lists for the first day. Now, how far would that extend? And my question was whether that would cover or not cover potential targets, such as crossroads around Gracac or in Gracac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, for sure, for instance, at a distance of six kilometres, that range, with 128-millimetre mortars and rocket-launchers, and maybe at a greater distance. But at this point, Your Honours, it's really difficult for me, because when I demobilised, I did a lot of other types of work, and I couldn't really be more technical. I have prepared for this testimony, but a lot of time has elapsed, and I couldn't be more specific and technical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us at what time on the 7th, if it was on the 7th, you arrived in Donji Lapac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. It was around 1400 hours, I'm pretty sure, maybe 1430, from the direction of Gornji Lapac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what did you observe when you entered Donji Lapac, in terms of destruction? Was there a lot of destruction, buildings, houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, not really. When I entered, I saw smoke. I think a building was still on fire, it was burning, but some 10 or 15 minutes later I found out that it was actually the police station building. As for others -- other features, well, there was some trucks, torched trucks, that were on the side of the road, but I didn't see any burned or torched buildings. The roofs were still on, intact. There was glass, there was a lot of shattered, broken glass, but I didn't see any buildings destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you'd say apart from this police station which was on fire, that there was no major damage to other houses or constructions, apart from windows broken, but not, well, let's say, corner of a house, what disappeared, or a roof, or major damage to the walls? And I'm not talking about bullet impacts, but about real holes in the walls. There was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I didn't really see large-scale destruction. I would have noticed it, for sure. There was the usual damage, usual for such operations, so there wasn't major destruction. There weren't roofs pulled down, and, after all, the roads were clear. They were passable in Donji Lapac, so they weren't blocked with debris.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When did you leave Donji Lapac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, probably already 30 to 40 minutes later, when I received an order from Commander -- from the commander, from my commander, General Markac, to gather my men, all the men I could, and to move on forward to the state border, and to set up a blockade to prevent a counter blow. This was the axis Donji Lapac-Boricevac-Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you return to Donji Lapac at a later stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that same evening, certainly, I'm sure not. The next day, also I'm sure I didn't. Maybe on the 9th, but I think not even on the 9th did I go to Donji Lapac; rather, I just went to Boricevac, where I had a meeting. The logistics base -- we didn't have anything in Donji Lapac after I left with the brunt of the forces towards Kulen Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you come -- did you go through Donji Lapac at any later stage, which would have allowed you to observe whether the damage was still the same as it was when you arrived there on the 7th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if you can believe me, I can't recall, and I cannot even try and picture this in my mind, the events after the 9th, when I was at the closest point to Donji Lapac, some five kilometres off, because I had great difficulties in maintaining or keeping the front-line unbreached, and whenever I needed something or whatever I needed would be brought to the headquarters where I was at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Sacic, I have no further questions for you, and neither have my colleagues at this moment. Looking at the clock, we have seven minutes left. Is it of any use to start cross-examination, or should we give up the seven minutes?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'd suggest, Mr. President, to start tomorrow. That might be more practical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if there's no objection to that. First of all, I'd like to ask the usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom. Mr. Sacic, we'd like to see you back tomorrow at quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon, and that would be in Courtroom -- Madam Registrar? In this same Courtroom I. I again want to instruct you, and I do instruct you, not to speak with anyone about your testimony, whether the testimony already given or still to be given. Would you please follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I inquire with the parties whether now knowing what the examination by the Chamber covered, whether they could give already an indication as to how much time they would need for cross?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe, for me, it would be about two to three sessions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two to three sessions. Looking at the Defence, Mr. Mikulicic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I presume I will need one session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: One session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we don't plan any questions at this point. But if something develops, I'll certainly bring it to the Chamber's attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So the overall estimate is now four to five sessions, which opens a possibility that we could finish with the witness in two days. We then adjourn for the day, and we'll resume tomorrow, Wednesday, the 24th of March, quarter past 2.00, Courtroom I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 24th day of March, 2010, at 2.15 p.m. 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.55 p.m.,
